Reference: Hsiao, Moscona and Sastry (2026)

Model Setting

The paper asks whether governments systematically intervene in agricultural markets when climate extremes hit, why they do so, and what this implies for global adaptation to a warming world. The motivating case is India's wheat export ban of May 2022, announced after a heat wave cut output by about 10 percent: it protected Indian consumers, was attacked as "antifarmer" at home, and pushed world wheat prices up by 6 percent. The authors build a global panel of agricultural policy and extreme heat exposure by country, crop and year since 1980 and establish two facts with opposite signs. Extreme heat that hits domestic production leads to consumer-assisting policy that lowers domestic prices relative to world prices; extreme heat that hits foreign production leads to producer-assisting policy that raises them. A model in the tradition of Grossman and Helpman (1994), Goldberg and Maggi (1999) and Maggi and Rodriguez-Clare (2000), in which a government sets a border tax to maximize a weighted sum of consumer surplus, producer surplus and government revenue, rationalizes both facts: a sufficiently redistribution-focused government moves policy with the country's self-sufficiency, which domestic and foreign shocks push in opposite directions. Finally, an empirical equilibrium model built directly on the regression estimates quantifies who gains and who loses from the policy responses: domestic consumers are shielded, domestic producers and foreign consumers lose, and the global incidence is regressive.

Data and Measurement

Policy is measured with the nominal rate of assistance (NRA) from the World Bank's Distortions to Agricultural Incentives project (Anderson and Valenzuela 2008), an unbalanced panel of 79 agricultural products and 81 countries from 1955 to 2011 that covers over 85 percent of global agricultural production. For crop kkk in country ℓ\ellℓ at time ttt:

NRAℓkt=pℓkt−pktIpktI(9.2.4.1)\text{NRA}_{\ell kt}=\frac{p_{\ell kt}-p^I_{kt}}{p^I_{kt}} \tag{9.2.4.1}NRAℓkt​=pktI​pℓkt​−pktI​​(9.2.4.1)

where pℓktp_{\ell kt}pℓkt​ is the distorted domestic price per unit of production and pktIp^I_{kt}pktI​ the undistorted free-market international price, which is unobserved. Positive values are producer assistance (domestic prices above free-market levels) and negative values are consumer assistance. In practice the NRA is built from total assistance paid to producers relative to the value of production, so it captures border taxes, quantity restrictions such as export bans (through the induced price wedge), domestic output and input subsidies, and temporary measures not set by legislation. Independent data on tariffs (UN TRAINS) and on import and export restrictions (Global Trade Alert, from 2008) are used to separate policy levers. Across the 642 markets (country-crop pairs) in the sample, 52 percent have an average price wedge larger than 15 percent in absolute value and 9 percent have a wedge larger than 80 percent.

Shocks are measured by crop-specific extreme heat. Each country ℓ\ellℓ is partitioned into grid cells c∈ℓc\in\ellc∈ℓ, and following Moscona and Sastry (2023):

ExtremeHeatℓkt=∑c∈ℓAreack∑c′∈ℓAreac′k⋅DegreeDaysct(Tkmax⁡)(9.2.4.2)\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}=\sum_{c\in\ell}\frac{\text{Area}_{ck}}{\sum_{c'\in\ell}\text{Area}_{c'k}}\cdot\text{DegreeDays}_{ct}\left(T_k^{\max}\right) \tag{9.2.4.2}ExtremeHeatℓkt​=c∈ℓ∑​∑c′∈ℓ​Areac′k​Areack​​⋅DegreeDaysct​(Tkmax​)(9.2.4.2)

where DegreeDaysct(x)\text{DegreeDays}_{ct}(x)DegreeDaysct​(x) is total degree days in excess of threshold xxx in cell ccc at time ttt (from ERA5 temperatures), Tkmax⁡T_k^{\max}Tkmax​ is the maximum optimal growing temperature of crop kkk from the FAO EcoCrop database, and Areack\text{Area}_{ck}Areack​ is the area growing crop kkk in cell ccc from EarthStat (circa 2000). The measure varies across crops within a country-year because crops are grown in different places and tolerate heat differently. It is validated on FAOSTAT yields:

log⁡(yieldℓkt)=f(ExtremeHeatℓkt)+γℓt+δkt+μℓk+ϵℓkt(9.2.4.3)\log(\text{yield}_{\ell kt})=f(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})+\gamma_{\ell t}+\delta_{kt}+\mu_{\ell k}+\epsilon_{\ell kt} \tag{9.2.4.3}log(yieldℓkt​)=f(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)+γℓt​+δkt​+μℓk​+ϵℓkt​(9.2.4.3)

where fff is a set of indicators for quartiles of ExtremeHeatℓkt\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}ExtremeHeatℓkt​ (the first quartile is omitted) and γℓt\gamma_{\ell t}γℓt​, δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​, μℓk\mu_{\ell k}μℓk​ are country-year, crop-year and country-crop fixed effects. Yields in the top heat quartile are over 20 percent lower than in the bottom quartile. The function fff is later reused as the damage function in the quantification.

Empirical Evidence: Domestic Shocks

The main estimating equation replaces the outcome with policy:

NRAℓkt=g(ExtremeHeatℓkt)+γℓt+δkt+μℓk+ϵℓkt(9.2.4.4)\text{NRA}_{\ell kt}=g(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})+\gamma_{\ell t}+\delta_{kt}+\mu_{\ell k}+\epsilon_{\ell kt} \tag{9.2.4.4}NRAℓkt​=g(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)+γℓt​+δkt​+μℓk​+ϵℓkt​(9.2.4.4)

where ggg is again spanned by quartile indicators and standard errors are clustered by market. Identification comes from differential exposure of crops within country-years, net of country-specific and crop-specific trends. The findings are:

  • Pro-consumer response: in the full sample, fourth-quartile relative to first-quartile heat lowers the NRA by 0.07 (0.09 in-sample standard deviations), i.e. a 7 percent fall in domestic relative to international prices. For the ten major crops of Costinot, Donaldson and Smith (2016) the effect is 28 percentage points (0.36 standard deviations), and for staple crops (maize, soybeans, rice, wheat, tomatoes, potatoes, onions) it is 32 percentage points (0.40 standard deviations): a country with no initial distortion would implement a 32 percent consumer subsidy. The fourth-quartile effect is significantly larger than the third-quartile effect, and there is no significant effect for cash crops.

  • Border policies: decomposing the NRA, the response is driven by output policies at the border, is weaker for farm-gate output policies, and is absent for input policies. For major crops the fourth-quartile coefficient is −0.285-0.285−0.285 in the full sample, −0.356-0.356−0.356 for net importers and −0.222-0.222−0.222 for net exporters. Tariffs fall by −0.036-0.036−0.036 overall and by −0.069-0.069−0.069 for net importers, with essentially no effect (−0.003-0.003−0.003) for net exporters. The count of export restrictions net of import restrictions (at the country-pair level, with country-pair fixed effects) rises by 0.112 overall and by 0.222 for net exporters. All markets respond in the pro-consumer direction, but the lever depends on the trade position.

  • Aggregation: a country-year version with calorie-weighted crops gives quantitatively similar estimates, so cross-crop interactions are small on average.

Empirical Evidence: Foreign Shocks, Dynamics and Heterogeneity

Foreign shocks are measured in two main ways. The first is a leave-one-out global average over grid cells in all countries LLL except ℓ\ellℓ:

ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt=∑c∈L∖ℓAreack∑c′∈L∖ℓAreac′k⋅DegreeDaysct(Tkmax⁡)(9.2.4.5)\text{ForeignExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}=\sum_{c\in L\setminus\ell}\frac{\text{Area}_{ck}}{\sum_{c'\in L\setminus\ell}\text{Area}_{c'k}}\cdot\text{DegreeDays}_{ct}\left(T_k^{\max}\right) \tag{9.2.4.5}ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt​=c∈L∖ℓ∑​∑c′∈L∖ℓ​Areac′k​Areack​​⋅DegreeDaysct​(Tkmax​)(9.2.4.5)

The second weights trading partners' shocks by import and export shares from the decade preceding the analysis:

ForeignExtremeHeatℓktM=∑ℓ′≠ℓImportShareℓ′ℓk⋅ExtremeHeatℓ′ktForeignExtremeHeatℓktX=∑ℓ′≠ℓExportShareℓ′ℓk⋅ExtremeHeatℓ′kt(9.2.4.6)\begin{aligned} \text{ForeignExtremeHeat}^M_{\ell kt}&=\sum_{\ell'\neq\ell}\text{ImportShare}_{\ell'\ell k}\cdot\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell'kt}\\ \text{ForeignExtremeHeat}^X_{\ell kt}&=\sum_{\ell'\neq\ell}\text{ExportShare}_{\ell'\ell k}\cdot\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell'kt} \end{aligned} \tag{9.2.4.6}ForeignExtremeHeatℓktM​ForeignExtremeHeatℓktX​​=ℓ′=ℓ∑​ImportShareℓ′ℓk​⋅ExtremeHeatℓ′kt​=ℓ′=ℓ∑​ExportShareℓ′ℓk​⋅ExtremeHeatℓ′kt​​(9.2.4.6)

with the import-weighted version assigned to net importing markets and the export-weighted version to net exporting markets. The augmented regression is:

NRAℓkt=g(ExtremeHeatℓkt)+h(ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt)+γℓt+δkt+μℓk+ϵℓkt(9.2.4.7)\text{NRA}_{\ell kt}=g(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})+h(\text{ForeignExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})+\gamma_{\ell t}+\delta_{kt}+\mu_{\ell k}+\epsilon_{\ell kt} \tag{9.2.4.7}NRAℓkt​=g(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)+h(ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt​)+γℓt​+δkt​+μℓk​+ϵℓkt​(9.2.4.7)

where hhh is also spanned by quartile indicators, and δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ is dropped when the leave-one-out measure (which varies only by crop-year) is used. With the global measure and all crops, the fourth-quartile domestic coefficient is −0.098-0.098−0.098 while the fourth-quartile foreign coefficient is 0.197: a top-quartile foreign shock raises domestic relative to international prices by 19.7 percent. For major crops the two coefficients are −0.267-0.267−0.267 and 0.246. With trade-weighted shocks and all two-way fixed effects they are −0.136-0.136−0.136 and 0.085 (all crops) and −0.254-0.254−0.254 and 0.125 (major crops). The NRA also rises with international prices, more strongly and precisely when prices are instrumented with foreign extreme heat. Thus domestic and foreign shocks induce opposite policy responses, which contradicts both a "contagion of food restrictions" view and a view in which governments simply protect consumers whenever food is scarce.

Dynamics are estimated with leads and lags:

NRAℓkt=∑s=−23g(EHℓk,t−s)+∑s=−23h(FEHℓk,t−s)+γℓt+δkt+μℓk+ϵℓkt(9.2.4.8)\text{NRA}_{\ell kt}=\sum_{s=-2}^{3}g(\text{EH}_{\ell k,t-s})+\sum_{s=-2}^{3}h(\text{FEH}_{\ell k,t-s})+\gamma_{\ell t}+\delta_{kt}+\mu_{\ell k}+\epsilon_{\ell kt} \tag{9.2.4.8}NRAℓkt​=s=−2∑3​g(EHℓk,t−s​)+s=−2∑3​h(FEHℓk,t−s​)+γℓt​+δkt​+μℓk​+ϵℓkt​(9.2.4.8)

where EHℓk,t−s\text{EH}_{\ell k,t-s}EHℓk,t−s​ and FEHℓk,t−s\text{FEH}_{\ell k,t-s}FEHℓk,t−s​ are domestic and (trade-weighted) foreign exposure in year t−st-st−s, so that sss counts years since the shock (the paper's equation prints t+st+st+s), with separate quartile coefficients for each sss. Coefficients on future shocks are close to zero (no anticipation); the domestic effect stays negative and significant three years after the shock, and the foreign effect lasts one additional year. At decadal frequency, each additional year of fourth-quartile domestic heat lowers the average decadal NRA of major crops by 0.055 and each year of foreign heat raises it by 0.023; ten such domestic years (8 percent of the sample) imply a 55 percent pro-consumer wedge, or 0.80 standard deviations of decadal NRA (0.69). Long-run responses are thus at least as large as short-run ones.

Heterogeneity points to political and fiscal mechanisms:

  • Elections: for major crops the fourth-quartile effect is −0.386-0.386−0.386 in the year of or before an election against −0.076-0.076−0.076 otherwise (five times as large); for staples it is −0.441-0.441−0.441 against −0.089-0.089−0.089.

  • Fiscal constraints: responses are substantially muted when central government debt relative to GDP is high.

  • Country characteristics (standardized interactions with fourth-quartile heat): no heterogeneity by polity score or by total or per capita GDP; weaker responses in more agricultural countries (0.175), stronger in more urban countries (−0.254-0.254−0.254) and in countries that import a larger share of their food (−0.792-0.792−0.792). Responses also appear stronger for crops consumed disproportionately by the poor.

Model: Market and Government

The model considers the market for one agricultural commodity from the perspective of a home country that is a net exporter (all results extend to a net importer facing isoelastic foreign net supply). Domestic demand, domestic supply and foreign net demand ("exports") are isoelastic:

q=Q(p)=p−εdy=Y(p,ω)=ωpεsx=X(p,ω′)=ω′p−εx(9.2.4.9)\begin{aligned} q&=Q(p)=p^{-\varepsilon_d}\\ y&=Y(p,\omega)=\omega p^{\varepsilon_s}\\ x&=X(p,\omega')=\omega'p^{-\varepsilon_x} \end{aligned} \tag{9.2.4.9}qyx​=Q(p)=p−εd​=Y(p,ω)=ωpεs​=X(p,ω′)=ω′p−εx​​(9.2.4.9)

where εd>0\varepsilon_d>0εd​>0, εs>0\varepsilon_s>0εs​>0 and εx>0\varepsilon_x>0εx​>0 are the elasticities of demand, supply and export demand, ω\omegaω is a productivity shock that increases domestic production, and ω′\omega'ω′ is a shock that increases export demand. A domestic heat shock is a low ω\omegaω; a foreign heat shock is a high ω′\omega'ω′. The paper assumes εd<εx<∞\varepsilon_d<\varepsilon_x<\inftyεd​<εx​<∞ and εx>1\varepsilon_x>1εx​>1, so foreign demand is sufficiently but not infinitely elastic and the country has some market power. The government sets an ad valorem border tax α>−1\alpha>-1α>−1 that drives a wedge between the domestic equilibrium price p∗p^*p∗ and the international price pIp^IpI, and the market clears:

p∗=(1+α)pI,Y(p∗,ω)=Q(p∗)+X(p∗1+α,ω′)(9.2.4.10)p^*=(1+\alpha)p^I,\qquad Y(p^*,\omega)=Q(p^*)+X\left(\frac{p^*}{1+\alpha},\omega'\right) \tag{9.2.4.10}p∗=(1+α)pI,Y(p∗,ω)=Q(p∗)+X(1+αp∗​,ω′)(9.2.4.10)

A positive α\alphaα is an export subsidy and a negative α\alphaα an export tax, and α\alphaα corresponds exactly to the NRA. Government expenditure is αpI=α1+αp∗\alpha p^I=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}p^*αpI=1+αα​p∗ per exported unit. The government chooses policy to maximize a weighted sum of consumer surplus, producer surplus and government revenue:

α∗∈arg⁡max⁡α∈[−1,∞){λC∫p∗pˉQ(p) dp+λP∫0p∗Y(p,ω) dp−λGα1+αp∗X(p∗1+α,ω′)}s.t.p∗=P∗(α,ω,ω′)(9.2.4.11)\alpha^*\in\arg\max_{\alpha\in[-1,\infty)}\left\{\lambda^C\int_{p^*}^{\bar{p}}Q(p)\,dp+\lambda^P\int_{0}^{p^*}Y(p,\omega)\,dp-\lambda^G\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}p^*X\left(\frac{p^*}{1+\alpha},\omega'\right)\right\}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p^*=P^*(\alpha,\omega,\omega') \tag{9.2.4.11}α∗∈argα∈[−1,∞)max​{λC∫p∗pˉ​​Q(p)dp+λP∫0p∗​Y(p,ω)dp−λG1+αα​p∗X(1+αp∗​,ω′)}s.t.p∗=P∗(α,ω,ω′)(9.2.4.11)

The problem is assumed quasi-concave in α\alphaα. Foreign consumers and producers receive no weight.

The reduced-form objective is derived from an economy with heterogeneous households i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\dots,N\}i∈{1,…,N} and two goods, the agricultural good and a numeraire ("money"). A household that consumes qiq_iqi​, produces yiy_iyi​ and consumes ziz_izi​ of the numeraire has payoff:

where μi\mu_iμi​ and ψi\psi_iψi​ are household iii's shares of domestic consumption and production. If λi=1/N\lambda_i=1/Nλi​=1/N for all iii, then λC=λP=λG\lambda^C=\lambda^P=\lambda^GλC=λP=λG. So λC\lambda^CλC is high when the government's preferred households consume much of the good (staples eaten by the poor under a progressive government), λP\lambda^PλP is high when they produce it (smallholders), and λG\lambda^GλG is high when existing transfers already reach them, or when the government wants to move resources to groups outside agricultural markets; it is low when transfers are a "leaky bucket" (Okun 1975).

Optimal Policy and Comparative Statics

Optimal policy depends on the elasticities, the weights, and one equilibrium sufficient statistic, the self-sufficiency ratio r=y/qr=y/qr=y/q. Proposition 1 states:

α∗=1εx(εx(λPr+λG(1−r)−λC)−λG(εsr+εd)λG(εsr+εd)−(λPr+λG(1−r)−λC))(9.2.4.14)\alpha^*=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_x}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_x\left(\lambda^Pr+\lambda^G(1-r)-\lambda^C\right)-\lambda^G(\varepsilon_sr+\varepsilon_d)}{\lambda^G(\varepsilon_sr+\varepsilon_d)-\left(\lambda^Pr+\lambda^G(1-r)-\lambda^C\right)}\right) \tag{9.2.4.14}α∗=εx​1​(λG(εs​r+εd​)−(λPr+λG(1−r)−λC)εx​(λPr+λG(1−r)−λC)−λG(εs​r+εd​)​)(9.2.4.14)

and α∗\alpha^*α∗ increases in λP\lambda^PλP and decreases in λC\lambda^CλC. In the utilitarian case λP=λC=λG\lambda^P=\lambda^C=\lambda^GλP=λC=λG the formula collapses to the inverse elasticity rule α∗=−1/εx\alpha^*=-1/\varepsilon_xα∗=−1/εx​: the country taxes trade in proportion to its ability to manipulate the terms of trade, and policy does not respond to shocks at all. Away from this case, shocks matter only through rrr. Definition 1 says the government is redistribution-focused in a market if:

εsλC+εdλPεs+εd>λG(9.2.4.15)\frac{\varepsilon_s\lambda^C+\varepsilon_d\lambda^P}{\varepsilon_s+\varepsilon_d}>\lambda^G \tag{9.2.4.15}εs​+εd​εs​λC+εd​λP​>λG(9.2.4.15)

and revenue-focused if the opposite inequality holds; the utilitarian government sits exactly at equality. Proposition 2: if the government is redistribution-focused, α∗\alpha^*α∗ increases in ω\omegaω and in ω′\omega'ω′; if it is revenue-focused, α∗\alpha^*α∗ decreases in ω\omegaω and in ω′\omega'ω′. The redistribution-focused case matches the data: a domestic heat shock (lower ω\omegaω) lowers the NRA, and a foreign heat shock (higher ω′\omega'ω′) raises it. Domestic and foreign supply disruptions have opposite effects because the first reduces self-sufficiency and the second increases it.

Two channels push in opposite directions after an adverse domestic supply shock.

  • Redistribution channel: shocks shift the incidence of prices between domestic agents and foreigners, who carry zero weight. A pro-consumer government taxes exports to lower domestic prices, which cross-subsidizes foreign producers through higher world prices; when domestic supply falls, exports fall, the leakage shrinks, and the export tax targets domestic consumers better, so the tax rises. A pro-producer government subsidizes exports; with less production the marginal return to producer price support falls, so the subsidy is cut. Either way policy becomes more pro-consumer.

  • Revenue channel: with low export volume, a marginal export tax raises little revenue and a marginal export subsidy costs little, which pushes toward lower taxes or higher subsidies, i.e. toward producers. Its strength rises with λG\lambda^GλG.

Definition 1 determines which channel dominates. The model also explains why responses are similar across importers and exporters and across rich and poor countries (average incentives, which set the level of α∗\alpha^*α∗, are distinct from marginal incentives), why staples respond more (higher λC\lambda^CλC), and why elections strengthen and debt weakens the response (stronger redistribution and revenue motives). Two alternatives, helping poor households with concave utility and stabilizing prices around a target, both predict the same response to domestic and foreign shocks, because either shock raises domestic prices; the data reject this.

Quantification: Empirical Equilibrium Model

The quantitative model stays close to the estimating equations. Demand and supply in each country ℓ\ellℓ, crop kkk and year ttt are:

where qℓkt0q^0_{\ell kt}qℓkt0​, yℓkt0y^0_{\ell kt}yℓkt0​ and αℓkt0\alpha^0_{\ell kt}αℓkt0​ are intercepts recovered as residuals and fff, ggg, hhh are the estimated damage and policy functions. Domestic prices are pℓkt=(1+αℓkt)pktIp_{\ell kt}=(1+\alpha_{\ell kt})p^I_{kt}pℓkt​=(1+αℓkt​)pktI​, and for each crop and year the international price clears the world market given exposure ωkt\omega_{kt}ωkt​ and policy αkt\alpha_{kt}αkt​ across countries:

where ΔxR\Delta x^RΔxR is the total effect under responsive policy, ΔxU\Delta x^UΔxU is the production effect with policy held fixed (unresponsive policy), and ΔxR−ΔxU\Delta x^R-\Delta x^UΔxR−ΔxU is the policy effect that works through induced policy changes. Standard errors use the delta method.

Quantification: Who Gains and Who Loses

  • Shocked markets (35 percent of markets): prices rise by 7.9 percent under unresponsive policy and 5.6 percent under responsive policy, so policy dampens price increases by 29 percent. Consumer surplus losses fall by 31 percent (a gain of 7.6 billion dollars per year). Producer surplus losses rise by 276 percent: without policy responses producers lose only 3.0 billion dollars per year, because inelastic demand lets prices spike and hedge output losses; policy responses add 8.4 billion dollars per year of producer losses.

  • Unshocked markets (65 percent): world prices rise as shocked countries restrict exports, and unshocked governments add pro-producer policy in response to the foreign shock. Price increases are amplified by 51 percent (4.7 percent under unresponsive against 7.0 percent under responsive policy); foreign consumers suffer 50 percent larger surplus losses and foreign producers enjoy 56 percent larger gains.

  • Efficiency: the world is already second-best. Policy responses magnify baseline distortions in 35 percent of markets and diminish them in 65 percent. Total welfare losses in shocked markets exceed 24 billion dollars per year but are similar with and without policy responses, and policy responses raise the volatility of prices and surplus.

  • Countries: policy responses improve utilitarian welfare in 40 percent of countries and reduce it in 60 percent, often by more than 25 percent of the no-response damage. Losses are larger where responses amplify baseline distortions (India, with pro-consumer policy at baseline) and turn into gains where amplification is limited (the United States).

  • Regressive incidence: countries most damaged by heat and the poorest countries are hurt by policy responses, while the least damaged and the richest are helped.

  • Global aggregates: heat shocks cut trade by 9.2 billion dollars per year under unresponsive policy, and the reduction is 96 percent larger under responsive policy, yet the effect on aggregate welfare is neutral because gains where distortions shrink offset losses where they grow.

The broader message is that economic policy is itself an endogenous margin of climate adaptation: climate change shifts food policy, and food policy redistributes, and for poor and heat-exposed countries worsens, the consequences of climate change.

This is the definition of the paper's policy outcome, the nominal rate of assistance. The index ℓ\ellℓ is a country, kkk a crop and ttt a year. The numerator is the gap between the distorted domestic producer price pℓktp_{\ell kt}pℓkt​ and the price pktIp^I_{kt}pktI​ that would prevail at the border without intervention, and dividing by pktIp^I_{kt}pktI​ makes the measure a unit-free proportional wedge. Rearranging gives the form used throughout the model:

pℓkt=(1+NRAℓkt)pktIp_{\ell kt}=\left(1+\text{NRA}_{\ell kt}\right)p^I_{kt}pℓkt​=(1+NRAℓkt​)pktI​

so the NRA is the ad valorem tariff-equivalent of all policies acting on the market. A value of 0.250.250.25 means domestic prices are 25 percent above free-market prices (producers are assisted, consumers are taxed); a value of −0.25-0.25−0.25 means domestic prices are 25 percent below (consumers are assisted). The lower bound is −1-1−1, a domestic price of zero; there is no upper bound.

The measure is deliberately agnostic about the instrument. A tariff, an export tax, an export ban or a production subsidy all show up as a price wedge, which is why the NRA picks up discretionary measures that statutory tariff data miss. The cost is that pktIp^I_{kt}pktI​ is not observed and must be constructed by the data builders from border prices adjusted for quality, transport and exchange-rate distortions, so the NRA contains measurement error. It is the dependent variable of equations (4), (7) and (8), it is the empirical counterpart of the border tax α\alphaα in equation (10), and it is the policy variable αℓkt\alpha_{\ell kt}αℓkt​ of the quantification in equation (17).

This defines the shock. Each country ℓ\ellℓ is cut into grid cells ccc, and the measure is a weighted average over cells of local heat that is harmful to crop kkk. The weight of cell ccc is its share of the country's total area planted with crop kkk, so the weights are nonnegative and sum to one:

∑c∈ℓAreack∑c′∈ℓAreac′k=1\sum_{c\in\ell}\frac{\text{Area}_{ck}}{\sum_{c'\in\ell}\text{Area}_{c'k}}=1c∈ℓ∑​∑c′∈ℓ​Areac′k​Areack​​=1

The heat variable is degree days above the crop-specific threshold Tkmax⁡T_k^{\max}Tkmax​. Schematically, with TcdT_{cd}Tcd​ the temperature in cell ccc on day ddd of year ttt,

DegreeDaysct(x)=∑d∈tmax⁡{Tcd−x, 0}\text{DegreeDays}_{ct}(x)=\sum_{d\in t}\max\left\{T_{cd}-x,\,0\right\}DegreeDaysct​(x)=d∈t∑​max{Tcd​−x,0}

so a day at 34 degrees contributes 4 degree days for a crop with a threshold of 30 and nothing for a crop with a threshold of 35. The units of the measure are therefore degree days per year, averaged over the land where the crop grows.

Two features matter for identification. First, the crop areas are fixed at their values around the year 2000, so the measure does not move when farmers relocate crops in response to weather or policy; only temperature realizations move it over time. Second, the measure varies across crops within the same country and year for two reasons: crops are planted in different cells, and they have different thresholds Tkmax⁡T_k^{\max}Tkmax​. This within-country-year variation is what survives the country-year fixed effects in equations (3), (4) and (7). The same formula, applied to cells outside the country, gives the foreign shock in equation (5), and country-level values are the building blocks of equation (6).

This is the first-stage or validation regression: it checks that the heat measure of equation (2) actually destroys output. The outcome is log yield (output per unit of land), so coefficients are approximately proportional changes. The function fff is a step function in the quartiles of the heat distribution with the first quartile as the omitted category:

f(ExtremeHeatℓkt)=∑j=24βj⋅1{ExtremeHeatℓkt∈quartile j}f(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})=\sum_{j=2}^{4}\beta_j\cdot\mathbf{1}\left\{\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}\in\text{quartile }j\right\}f(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)=j=2∑4​βj​⋅1{ExtremeHeatℓkt​∈quartile j}

Each βj\beta_jβj​ is the log yield difference between quartile jjj and the bottom quartile. Using indicators rather than a linear term lets the data reveal nonlinearity: heat damage is known to be convex, and the estimates show that the top quartile is where most of the damage occurs, with β4\beta_4β4​ below −0.2-0.2−0.2.

The three sets of fixed effects define the identifying variation. The country-year effect γℓt\gamma_{\ell t}γℓt​ absorbs anything common to all crops in a country and year (macroeconomic conditions, the overall weather of the year, national politics). The crop-year effect δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ absorbs global crop-specific movements such as world prices and technology. The country-crop effect μℓk\mu_{\ell k}μℓk​ absorbs permanent suitability of a country for a crop. What is left is whether a crop that is unusually heat-exposed, relative to other crops in the same country-year and relative to the same crop elsewhere, has unusually low yield. The estimated fff is later reused as the damage function that shifts supply in equation (16).

This is the main estimating equation. It has the same right-hand side as the yield regression in equation (3), but the outcome is now policy, the NRA of equation (1). The function ggg is again a set of quartile indicators with the bottom quartile omitted:

g(ExtremeHeatℓkt)=∑j=24θj⋅1{ExtremeHeatℓkt∈quartile j}g(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})=\sum_{j=2}^{4}\theta_j\cdot\mathbf{1}\left\{\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}\in\text{quartile }j\right\}g(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)=j=2∑4​θj​⋅1{ExtremeHeatℓkt​∈quartile j}

so θ4\theta_4θ4​ is the change in the price wedge, in units of the international price, when a market moves from the bottom to the top quartile of heat. A value of θ4=−0.28\theta_4=-0.28θ4​=−0.28 for major crops means that domestic prices fall by 28 percent of the international price relative to what they would otherwise have been: policy becomes more pro-consumer exactly when domestic supply is hit.

The fixed effects carry the identification. Because γℓt\gamma_{\ell t}γℓt​ is included, the comparison is across crops within a country and year, so a government-wide shift in trade stance, an election, a currency crisis or a general drought cannot explain the result. Because δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ is included, global movements in the price of a crop are removed, which matters since the unobserved pktIp^I_{kt}pktI​ sits in the denominator of the NRA. Because μℓk\mu_{\ell k}μℓk​ is included, permanent protection of particular crops is removed. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on these effects, year-to-year heat realizations are as good as random with respect to other determinants of policy. Standard errors are clustered by market (country-crop) to allow serial correlation in policy. This equation is extended with foreign shocks in equation (7), and ggg becomes the domestic policy function in equation (17).

This is the first measure of foreign shocks. It is the formula of equation (2) applied to a different set of cells: all cells in the set of countries LLL except those of country ℓ\ellℓ. The weights are shares of the world area of crop kkk outside ℓ\ellℓ, so the measure is the average harmful heat experienced by the rest of the world's production of crop kkk in year ttt. It is called a leave-one-out measure because the own country is excluded, which prevents the foreign shock from mechanically containing the domestic shock.

A useful way to read it is as an area-weighted average of the country-level measures of equation (2). Writing Aℓ′kA_{\ell' k}Aℓ′k​ for the total crop area of country ℓ′\ell'ℓ′,

ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt=∑ℓ′≠ℓAℓ′k∑ℓ′′≠ℓAℓ′′k⋅ExtremeHeatℓ′kt,Aℓ′k=∑c∈ℓ′Areack\text{ForeignExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}=\sum_{\ell'\neq\ell}\frac{A_{\ell' k}}{\sum_{\ell''\neq\ell}A_{\ell'' k}}\cdot\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell' kt},\qquad A_{\ell' k}=\sum_{c\in\ell'}\text{Area}_{ck}ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt​=ℓ′=ℓ∑​∑ℓ′′=ℓ​Aℓ′′k​Aℓ′k​​⋅ExtremeHeatℓ′kt​,Aℓ′k​=c∈ℓ′∑​Areack​

which shows that large producers dominate the measure. The economic content is that it proxies for a contraction of world supply and hence for upward pressure on the international price.

The limitation is that for a small country the measure is almost the same number as for every other country: it varies essentially only by crop and year. It is therefore nearly collinear with the crop-year fixed effect δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​, which must be dropped when this measure enters equation (7). Without δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​, identification relies on time variation within a market, so any other global crop-year shock correlated with global heat is a threat. That is the reason for the trade-weighted alternative in equation (6).

These are the trade-weighted foreign shocks. Both lines are weighted sums of the partner-country heat measures of equation (2), and they differ only in the weights. In the first line, ImportShareℓ′ℓk\text{ImportShare}_{\ell'\ell k}ImportShareℓ′ℓk​ is the share of country ℓ\ellℓ's imports of crop kkk that come from partner ℓ′\ell'ℓ′; the measure is the heat hitting the countries that ℓ\ellℓ buys from. In the second line, ExportShareℓ′ℓk\text{ExportShare}_{\ell'\ell k}ExportShareℓ′ℓk​ is the bilateral export share linking ℓ\ellℓ and ℓ′\ell'ℓ′ for crop kkk; the measure is the heat hitting the countries that ℓ\ellℓ sells to. Within each definition the weights sum to one over partners,

∑ℓ′≠ℓImportShareℓ′ℓk=1,∑ℓ′≠ℓExportShareℓ′ℓk=1\sum_{\ell'\neq\ell}\text{ImportShare}_{\ell'\ell k}=1,\qquad\sum_{\ell'\neq\ell}\text{ExportShare}_{\ell'\ell k}=1ℓ′=ℓ∑​ImportShareℓ′ℓk​=1,ℓ′=ℓ∑​ExportShareℓ′ℓk​=1

so each measure is an average and has the same units as the domestic shock.

This is a shift-share design. The shifts are the partners' heat realizations, which are plausibly random; the shares are measured in the decade before the estimation sample and are held fixed, so they cannot respond to the shocks or to the policies under study. The gain over equation (5) is that two countries facing the same crop in the same year now have different foreign exposure because they trade with different partners. The crop-year fixed effect δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ can therefore stay in equation (7), and identification no longer rests on global time-series variation. The import-weighted version is assigned to net importing markets and the export-weighted version to net exporting markets, since these are the partners whose supply conditions move the prices that the market actually faces. In terms of the model, both correspond to a rise in the foreign shifter ω′\omega'ω′ of equation (9). The trade-weighted version is also the one used in the dynamic specification (8) and in the quantification.

This regression adds the foreign shock to equation (4). The function hhh is, like ggg, a set of quartile indicators with the bottom quartile omitted:

h(ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt)=∑j=24ϕj⋅1{ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt∈quartile j}h(\text{ForeignExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})=\sum_{j=2}^{4}\phi_j\cdot\mathbf{1}\left\{\text{ForeignExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt}\in\text{quartile }j\right\}h(ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt​)=j=2∑4​ϕj​⋅1{ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt​∈quartile j}

The coefficient ϕ4\phi_4ϕ4​ is the change in the NRA when foreign exposure moves from its bottom to its top quartile, holding domestic exposure and the fixed effects constant, and θ4\theta_4θ4​ in ggg is the analogous domestic effect holding foreign exposure constant. Including both matters because heat is spatially correlated: a hot year at home tends to be a hot year abroad, so omitting one shock would bias the coefficient on the other toward a mixture of the two.

When the leave-one-out measure of equation (5) is used, δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ is dropped and ϕj\phi_jϕj​ is identified from time variation within markets. When the trade-weighted measures of equation (6) are used, all three sets of fixed effects are kept and ϕj\phi_jϕj​ is identified from differences in partner composition across countries within a crop-year.

The key result is a sign pattern: θ4<0\theta_4<0θ4​<0 and ϕ4>0\phi_4>0ϕ4​>0. Both shocks make the crop scarcer and raise its price at home, yet policy moves in opposite directions. This is what a theory based only on protecting consumers from high prices, or on stabilizing prices, cannot produce, and it is what the model delivers through the self-sufficiency ratio in equations (14) and (15): a domestic shock lowers self-sufficiency while a foreign shock raises it. The estimated ggg and hhh are used directly as the policy rule in equation (17).

This is the dynamic version of equation (7). Domestic exposure EH\text{EH}EH and trade-weighted foreign exposure FEH\text{FEH}FEH enter at several dates around year ttt, and each date has its own set of quartile coefficients. The notation g(⋅)g(\cdot)g(⋅) inside the sum is shorthand; written out, the domestic part is

∑s=−23gs(EHℓk,t−s),gs(EHℓk,t−s)=∑j=24θj,s⋅1{EHℓk,t−s∈quartile j}\sum_{s=-2}^{3}g_s(\text{EH}_{\ell k,t-s}),\qquad g_s(\text{EH}_{\ell k,t-s})=\sum_{j=2}^{4}\theta_{j,s}\cdot\mathbf{1}\left\{\text{EH}_{\ell k,t-s}\in\text{quartile }j\right\}s=−2∑3​gs​(EHℓk,t−s​),gs​(EHℓk,t−s​)=j=2∑4​θj,s​⋅1{EHℓk,t−s​∈quartile j}

and similarly for hhh with coefficients ϕj,s\phi_{j,s}ϕj,s​. This is a distributed-lag, event-study style specification: because all dates are included jointly, each coefficient is the effect of a shock at that date holding shocks at the other dates fixed.

The coefficients serve two purposes. Those on shocks that occur after the policy is observed are placebo tests: weather that has not yet happened should not move current policy unless there are pre-trends or anticipation, and these coefficients are close to zero. Those on past shocks trace out persistence: the domestic effect is still negative three years after the shock and the foreign effect lasts one year beyond impact.

A note on the indexing. Exposure is dated t−st-st−s, so sss counts years elapsed since the shock: s=−2,−1s=-2,-1s=−2,−1 are shocks that have not yet happened (leads) and s=1,2,3s=1,2,3s=1,2,3 are past shocks (lags). The paper's equation prints t+st+st+s, which read literally gives two lags and three leads and does not match the reported results (two placebo leads, and effects up to three years after the shock). The trade-weighted foreign measure is used so that δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ can be retained alongside all leads and lags.

These three curves are the primitives of the theoretical model: domestic demand, domestic supply, and foreign net demand for the home country's exports. All are isoelastic, so each elasticity is a constant:

−dlog⁡Qdlog⁡p=εd,∂log⁡Y∂log⁡p=εs,−∂log⁡X∂log⁡p=εx-\frac{d\log Q}{d\log p}=\varepsilon_d,\qquad\frac{\partial\log Y}{\partial\log p}=\varepsilon_s,\qquad-\frac{\partial\log X}{\partial\log p}=\varepsilon_x−dlogpdlogQ​=εd​,∂logp∂logY​=εs​,−∂logp∂logX​=εx​

The scale of demand is normalized to one, which is without loss of generality given free units for quantity and price. The shifter ω\omegaω scales domestic supply proportionally at every price, so a domestic heat shock is a fall in ω\omegaω. The shifter ω′\omega'ω′ scales foreign net demand; a heat shock abroad reduces foreign production, raises what foreigners want to buy from home at any given price, and so is a rise in ω′\omega'ω′. Note that XXX is evaluated at the international price, while QQQ and YYY are evaluated at the domestic price; the two differ by the policy wedge in equation (10).

The functional form buys tractability: with constant elasticities the first-order condition of the government in equation (11) depends on the equilibrium only through the ratio r=y/qr=y/qr=y/q, which is what makes the closed form in equation (14) possible. It rules out choke prices, satiation and elasticities that vary along the curves.

The restrictions on the elasticities have clear roles. A finite εx\varepsilon_xεx​ means the country faces a downward-sloping export demand curve and can affect its terms of trade; as εx→∞\varepsilon_x\to\inftyεx​→∞ it becomes a price taker. The condition εx>1\varepsilon_x>1εx​>1 is the usual requirement for a monopolist-type optimum to exist, because the optimal export tax is 1/εx1/\varepsilon_x1/εx​ in the benchmark case and must be below one. The condition εx>εd\varepsilon_x>\varepsilon_dεx​>εd​ ensures that a positive domestic supply shock raises self-sufficiency, which is used in the derivation attached to equation (15). The same curves reappear in log form, with heterogeneous intercepts, in equation (16).

The first equality is a no-arbitrage condition. Let α\alphaα be an ad valorem export subsidy paid on the international price (an export tax if negative). A trader who buys one unit at home at p∗p^*p∗ and sells it abroad receives pIp^IpI from the foreign buyer plus αpI\alpha p^IαpI from the government. The second equality is market clearing for domestic output: production equals domestic consumption plus exports, where foreigners buy at pI=p∗/(1+α)p^I=p^*/(1+\alpha)pI=p∗/(1+α). This is the government's problem. It chooses the border tax α\alphaα to maximize a weighted sum of three money-metric objects, taking into account that the domestic price responds through the equilibrium mapping P∗P^*P∗ derived from equation (10).

The first term is consumer surplus, the area under the demand curve above the price. The weights λC\lambda^CλC, λP\lambda^PλP and λG\lambda^GλG are the value the government places on a dollar in the hands of consumers, producers and the treasury. This is the political-economy objective of the protection-for-sale literature in reduced form; equation (13) shows how it arises from Pareto weights on households. Foreigners receive zero weight, so the government is willing to shift the burden of its policy onto them. With equal weights the problem is that of a national-income-maximizing planner with market power. The constraint set α≥−1\alpha\geq-1α≥−1 keeps prices nonnegative, and quasi-concavity is assumed so that the first-order condition characterizes the optimum. That condition is solved in the derivation of equation (14).

This payoff is the micro-foundation of the supply and demand curves of equation (9) and of the government's objective in equation (11). These are the demand and supply curves of the quantitative model. They are the log versions of the isoelastic curves in equation (9), now with a separate intercept for every country, crop and year. Exponentiating,

qℓkt=qℓkt0 pℓkt−εd,yℓkt=yℓkt0 ef(ExtremeHeatℓkt) pℓktεsq_{\ell kt}=q^0_{\ell kt}\,p_{\ell kt}^{-\varepsilon_d},\qquad y_{\ell kt}=y^0_{\ell kt}\,e^{f(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})}\,p_{\ell kt}^{\varepsilon_s}qℓkt​=qℓkt0​pℓkt−εd​​,yℓkt​=yℓkt0​ef(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)pℓktεs​​

so the model's supply shifter is ω=yℓkt0ef\omega=y^0_{\ell kt}e^{f}ω=yℓkt0​ef: heat scales supply proportionally at every price, by the amount estimated in the yield regression of equation (3). Using the yield response as the output response assumes that planted area does not react to the shock within the year. A top-quartile value of f≈−0.2f\approx-0.2f≈−0.2 shifts supply down by about 18 percent at a given price; the equilibrium fall in quantity is smaller because the price rises.

The intercepts qℓkt0q^0_{\ell kt}qℓkt0​ and yℓkt0y^0_{\ell kt}yℓkt0​ are not estimated. They are backed out so that the curves pass exactly through the observed consumption, production and price of each market, given the calibrated elasticities and the estimated fff:

The model therefore reproduces the data by construction, and all unobserved determinants of demand and supply (income, tastes, technology, land) are held fixed in the intercepts when a counterfactual is run. The elasticities are calibrated rather than estimated: εd\varepsilon_dεd​ is around 0.4 on average and εs=1\varepsilon_s=1εs​=1. Inelastic demand is what makes prices spike after supply losses and partly insures producers, a force that shows up strongly in the results. These curves enter the world market clearing condition (18) and the surplus formulas in equation (19).

This is the policy rule of the quantitative model. Instead of solving the government's problem in equation (11) for each market, which would require knowing the weights λC\lambda^CλC, λP\lambda^PλP and λG\lambda^GλG everywhere, the authors let policy respond to shocks exactly as estimated in the regression of equation (7). The functions ggg and hhh are the estimated quartile step functions for domestic and foreign heat, and αℓkt\alpha_{\ell kt}αℓkt​ is the NRA.

The intercept is the part of observed policy not explained by current heat, recovered as a residual:

αℓkt0=αℓkt−g(ExtremeHeatℓkt)−h(ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt)\alpha^0_{\ell kt}=\alpha_{\ell kt}-g(\text{ExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})-h(\text{ForeignExtremeHeat}_{\ell kt})αℓkt0​=αℓkt​−g(ExtremeHeatℓkt​)−h(ForeignExtremeHeatℓkt​)

It contains everything that the fixed effects and the error absorb in equation (7): the permanent protection of a crop, the national policy stance of the year, and idiosyncratic policy changes. Under baseline exposure, policy is predicted by evaluating ggg and hhh at the baseline heat levels while keeping αℓkt0\alpha^0_{\ell kt}αℓkt0​ unchanged. Since ggg and hhh are zero in the bottom quartile, a market whose baseline exposure is in the bottom quartile has baseline policy equal to αℓkt0\alpha^0_{\ell kt}αℓkt0​.

The approach is a sufficient-statistic one. It is valid for any underlying model of government behaviour that generates the estimated responses, including the model of equations (11) to (15), and it avoids estimating political weights. The price paid is that the response functions are common across markets and are only reliable within the range of shocks observed in the data, and that policy is not allowed to respond to anything other than heat, for instance to other countries' policies beyond what hhh already captures. Policy maps into domestic prices through pℓkt=(1+αℓkt)pktIp_{\ell kt}=(1+\alpha_{\ell kt})p^I_{kt}pℓkt​=(1+αℓkt​)pktI​ and then into the market clearing condition (18).

The condition says that for each crop and year, world consumption equals world production. Its content is clearer once the pieces are substituted in. From equation (16) in levels and the price wedge pℓkt=(1+αℓkt)pktIp_{\ell kt}=(1+\alpha_{\ell kt})p^I_{kt}pℓkt​=(1+αℓkt​)pktI​, each country's quantities are functions of the single unknown pktIp^I_{kt}pktI​:

This expression shows the two forces in the results. A heat shock lowers efe^{f}ef in the denominator and raises the world price. A pro-consumer response (lower α\alphaα) in the shocked country raises its demand and lowers its supply, which raises the world price further; a pro-producer response (higher α\alphaα) elsewhere lowers the world price but raises the domestic price in those countries by more. The equation is the multi-country analogue of the market clearing condition in equation (10). In the implementation the fixed net supply of the rest of the world, the observed gap between production and consumption in the sample, is added as a constant to one side; the equation as written omits it.

The first line is accounting. Net imports are q−yq-yq−y; the positive-part operator (⋅)+(\cdot)^+(⋅)+ assigns the value of a positive gap to imports M\mathcal{M}M and of a negative gap to exports X\mathcal{X}X, so one of the two is always zero and Tℓkt=pℓkt∣qℓkt−yℓkt∣\mathcal{T}_{\ell kt}=p_{\ell kt}\left|q_{\ell kt}-y_{\ell kt}\right|Tℓkt​=pℓkt​∣qℓkt​−yℓkt​∣. Trade is valued at domestic prices.

Government revenue follows from the wedge. An importer (q>yq>yq>y) with α>0\alpha>0α>0 collects the tariff αpI=p−pI\alpha p^I=p-p^IαpI=p−pI on each of q−yq-yq−y imported units; an exporter with α>0\alpha>0α>0 pays the subsidy p−pIp-p^Ip−pI on each of y−qy-qy−q exported units. which for an exporter equals −α1+αp x-\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}p\,x−1+αα​px with x=y−qx=y-qx=y−q, the fiscal term in equation (11). Total welfare adds the three with equal weights, the utilitarian case λC=λP=λG\lambda^C=\lambda^P=\lambda^GλC=λP=λG of equation (11). Its price derivative at fixed pIp^IpI is −q+y+(q−y)+(p−pI) d(q−y)/dp=(p−pI) d(q−y)/dp-q+y+(q-y)+(p-p^I)\,d(q-y)/dp=(p-p^I)\,d(q-y)/dp−q+y+(q−y)+(p−pI)d(q−y)/dp=(p−pI)d(q−y)/dp, the familiar result that the marginal welfare cost of a distortion is proportional to the existing wedge. This is why policy responses that widen existing wedges reduce welfare and those that narrow them raise it.

These are the aggregation rules used to report results for groups of markets or for the world. The sums run over countries, crops and years in the group being reported.

The first is a Stone price index: a weighted average of log prices with weights equal to consumption expenditure shares eℓkt=pℓktqℓkt/Ee_{\ell kt}=p_{\ell kt}q_{\ell kt}/Eeℓkt​=pℓkt​qℓkt​/E, which sum to one. It is a geometric mean of prices,

p=∏ℓktpℓkt eℓktp=\prod_{\ell kt}p_{\ell kt}^{\,e_{\ell kt}}p=ℓkt∏​pℓkteℓkt​​

so a difference in ln⁡p\ln plnp between two scenarios is an expenditure-weighted average percentage price change. This is the number behind statements such as prices rising by 7.9 percent under unresponsive and 5.6 percent under responsive policy. Markets where consumers spend more count for more, which is the appropriate weighting for a cost-of-living interpretation. To first order, the change in the index approximates the proportional change in the cost of the observed consumption basket.

The second aggregates trade. Every unit traded is an export of one country and an import of another, and Tℓkt\mathcal{T}_{\ell kt}Tℓkt​ in equation (19) records each country's exports or imports, so summing over all countries counts each flow twice; the factor one half corrects this. The correction is exact only when the sum covers the whole world and both sides of each flow are valued alike; here each side is valued at its own domestic price, so it is an approximation.

The third simply adds money-metric surplus measures across markets. Unweighted addition means a dollar is valued equally whoever receives it, in any country, consistent with the utilitarian benchmark of equation (19); distributional statements are then made by reporting the sums separately for consumers, producers and governments and for different groups of countries. All three aggregates are evaluated under each scenario and differenced according to equation (21).

Let x(ω,α)x(\omega,\alpha)x(ω,α) be any equilibrium outcome computed from equations (16) to (20) under exposure ω\omegaω and policy α\alphaα. The observed world is (ω1,α1)(\omega_1,\alpha_1)(ω1​,α1​). The baseline world has minimal heat exposure ω0\omega_0ω0​ and the policy α0\alpha_0α0​ that equation (17) predicts at that exposure. The total damage from heat is the difference between the two. Add and subtract the outcome in the intermediate scenario (ω0,α1)(\omega_0,\alpha_1)(ω0​,α1​), in which exposure is at baseline but policy stays at its observed level:

x(ω1,α1)−x(ω0,α0)=x(ω1,α1)−x(ω0,α1)+x(ω0,α1)−x(ω0,α0)=[x(ω1,α1)−x(ω0,α1)]⏟ΔxU+[x(ω0,α1)−x(ω0,α0)]⏟ΔxR−ΔxU\begin{aligned} x(\omega_1,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_0)&=x(\omega_1,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_1)+x(\omega_0,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_0)\\ &=\underbrace{\left[x(\omega_1,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_1)\right]}_{\Delta x^U}+\underbrace{\left[x(\omega_0,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_0)\right]}_{\Delta x^R-\Delta x^U} \end{aligned}x(ω1​,α1​)−x(ω0​,α0​)​=x(ω1​,α1​)−x(ω0​,α1​)+x(ω0​,α1​)−x(ω0​,α0​)=ΔxU[x(ω1​,α1​)−x(ω0​,α1​)]​​+ΔxR−ΔxU[x(ω0​,α1​)−x(ω0​,α0​)]​​​

The identity is exact and holds for any outcome, whether or not xxx is linear. In the first bracket only exposure changes while policy is held at α1\alpha_1α1​: this is the effect of the shock when policy does not respond, the production effect. In the second bracket only policy changes, from α0\alpha_0α0​ to α1\alpha_1α1​, with exposure held at ω0\omega_0ω0​: this is the effect of the policy change that the shock induces. Since the left side is by definition ΔxR\Delta x^RΔxR, the second bracket equals ΔxR−ΔxU\Delta x^R-\Delta x^UΔxR−ΔxU, which explains its label.

Two remarks. First, the split is a path decomposition and is not unique when shocks and policy interact. One could instead pass through (ω1,α0)(\omega_1,\alpha_0)(ω1​,α0​):

x(ω1,α1)−x(ω0,α0)=[x(ω1,α0)−x(ω0,α0)]+[x(ω1,α1)−x(ω1,α0)]x(\omega_1,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_0)=\left[x(\omega_1,\alpha_0)-x(\omega_0,\alpha_0)\right]+\left[x(\omega_1,\alpha_1)-x(\omega_1,\alpha_0)\right]x(ω1​,α1​)−x(ω0​,α0​)=[x(ω1​,α0​)−x(ω0​,α0​)]+[x(ω1​,α1​)−x(ω1​,α0​)]

which holds policy at its baseline level in the production effect and evaluates the policy effect at observed exposure. The paper uses the first ordering, fixing unresponsive policy at the observed α1\alpha_1α1​. Second, percentage statements in the results are ratios of the two components: saying that policy dampens price increases by 29 percent means that (ΔxR−ΔxU)/ΔxU≈−0.29(\Delta x^R-\Delta x^U)/\Delta x^U\approx-0.29(ΔxR−ΔxU)/ΔxU≈−0.29 for the price index, since (5.6−7.9)/7.9≈−0.29(5.6-7.9)/7.9\approx-0.29(5.6−7.9)/7.9≈−0.29.
